compression.title: Anthropic Economic Index
compression.lede: is Anthropic's report series and open dataset on the use of its own model, Claude: another instance of Claude classifies sampled conversations to tasks, collaboration modes and "economic primitives", task success among them as "Claude’s assessment of whether Claude completes tasks" (reports; Labor Vector record).

sentences.text: The Anthropic Economic Index is a report series with data releases drawn from its operator's own product usage, a platform-specific observation of Anthropic's own product, Claude, published by Anthropic, and in the Labor Vector record's terms not a measure of AI use across providers but observed use on one provider's product (Labor Vector record).

Anthropic launched it on X as "a new initiative aimed at understanding AI's impact on the economy over time" whose first paper "analyzes millions of anonymized Claude conversations"; its home page heads it "Understanding AI’s effects on the economy" (last updated 26 June 2026) and describes "the shape of AI adoption across the world" as how people use Claude across US states and occupations; the dataset's README says it "provides insights into how AI is being incorporated into real-world tasks across the modern economy"; and the January 2026 report promises "a longitudinal view of AI's role in the economy".

Its operator is Anthropic's Economics team (Labor Vector record), and its series runs, by the README, from the initial release of 10 February 2025 "with O*NET task mappings, automation vs. augmentation data, and more", through the second release's paper "Which Economic Tasks are Performed with AI? Evidence from Millions of Claude Conversations" and the third report by Appel, McCrory, Tamkin, McCain, Neylon and Stern (arXiv, 19 November 2025), which Peter McCrory announced on LinkedIn as documenting "the contours of AI adoption across 150+ countries", to the sixth, "Cadences", of 26 June 2026: six reports (README; arXiv; Labor Vector record).

It observes the tasks people bring to Claude, mapped to the O*NET tasks of the occupations that typically perform them, on Claude.ai, Cowork, Claude Code and Anthropic's first-party API only (Labor Vector record); the June 2026 report defines its consumer data as chat and Cowork sessions on Claude.ai and the desktop app and its 1P API as traffic "distinct from both Anthropic's consumer-facing Claude.ai application and third-party platforms such as Amazon Bedrock or Google Cloud Vertex", and the third report scopes itself to "patterns of Claude usage over time".

Its unit is a sampled conversation or API record "classified by Claude to an O*NET task and to economic primitives" (Labor Vector record), and in the June 2026 report's words "transcripts are only read by another instance of Claude", which the Labor Vector record tags as "NOT independent of the provider"; since that report a slice of conversations is sampled every day, where earlier reports drew seven-day samples (June 2026 report; Labor Vector record).

The January 2026 report validated its classifiers against a human researcher on "a small set of transcripts in which users gave feedback", neither validation source "fully representative" of the traffic, and "mainly tested for directional accuracy", holding that simple primitives "even if somewhat noisy and not perfectly accurate by themselves" give signals together.

The archive holds that a model's score of its own output is preliminary and not self-certifying: #138 declines to claim that a system's self-audit is "independently authoritative" or its self-reported score "a validated measurement"; "A model auditing its own output may provide useful preliminary classification, but a metric-bearing audit requires traceable units and, where possible, external validation" (#766); a score "computed by the same system that generated the output requires external verification — by a second substrate, a human with source access, or a decoupled evaluation engine" (#780); and the check that does not run through a reasoner's own self-assessment is "application by another reasoner, a formal audit, or direct inspection of the inference path" (#777).

The archive's records give the grounds: a summarizer asked to score itself without a rubric "returns perfect scores every time" (#780); one substrate "gave itself a perfect score using the framework's own instruments" and, under instruction, scored the same composition PER ≈ 0.85 (#788); another's "preferred audit substantially exonerates itself" against a computed audit (#1470); and Anthropic's Constitutional AI, as #95 reports it, already "trains models to follow explicit principles through self-critique and revision, using AI-generated feedback rather than human labels" (#95).

The January 2026 report defines its "primitives" as "simple, foundational measures of how Claude is used, which we generate by asking Claude specific questions about anonymized Claude.ai and first-party (1P) API transcripts", on five dimensions (skills, complexity, autonomy, success, use case), with "AI autonomy" the degree to which users delegate decision-making to Claude; a Substack card reported the release as "introducing “economic primitives”".

"Task success measures Claude’s assessment of whether Claude completes tasks successfully", and serves to judge whether a task can be automated at all and how efficiently (January 2026 report); the Labor Vector record keeps the measure's assessor in a negative tag, "task success is Claude's assessment of whether Claude completes tasks", and records that the index does not answer "task success as judged by the user or by an external grader" (Labor Vector record).

The report finds that "Claude generally succeeds at the tasks it is given" and "struggles on more complex tasks", and bounds the finding itself: "users choose which tasks to bring to Claude", so observed success rates reflect "user judgment about what will work" and the cost of setting up the problem as well as capability (January 2026 report); on the archive's account task completion rates belong to the metrics that reward convergence: "Every UX metric — satisfaction scores, task completion rates, retention — improves when the model converges on the mode. Users do not notice tail loss." (#855).

The archive measures such labor from the commissioning side: Directionality of Semantic Labor is "the direction in which a synthetic system's labor flows relative to the task its user commissioned", across capacity, task-origin, retrieval, output and attribution, with the output "segmented into spans, each scored by function relative to the commissioned task", on the principle that "a system can produce fluent, well-attributed output while having abandoned the user's commissioned direction" (#771).

"A synthetic labor surface does not merely produce tokens; it allocates labor" (#771), and the Labor Vector record reads the index's collaboration modes and its autonomy and task-success primitives as "the nearest of the resource's measures to DSL's question of whether the system's labor advanced the commissioned task", classified "as Claude assesses its own completion", while none of the resources the census sets beside it records "from the commissioning side, whether the system's labor advanced the task the user set, or who receives the time it saves" (Labor Vector record); DSL bounds itself: it yields "a single reproducible value only on transcripts where the task vector is exogenous and fixed" and is frame-dependent on reflexive dialogue (#771).

The census asks of every resource "Who supplies the labor, who directs it, and who receives its gains" and places this one at labor performed with AI and the distribution of gains and losses (Labor Vector record); the index's oldest measure classifies conversations "into one of five interaction types, which we group into two broader categories: automation and augmentation" (January 2026 report), named "Directive", "Feedback Loop", "Task Iteration", "Learning" and "Validation" (June 2026 report) and glossed on the home page as "whether they prefer to collaborate with, or delegate to, Claude"; on the record's reading users and API customers bring the tasks that Claude performs, and the user directs, recorded as collaboration mode and delegated autonomy (Labor Vector record).

Directive delegation rose "from 27% to 39%" in the eight months before the third report, which found that "77% of business uses involve automation usage patterns, compared to about 50% for Claude.ai users" (third report); in November 2025 augmentation was again 52% of Claude.ai conversations against automation's 45%, while "automated use remains dominant in 1P API traffic" (January 2026 report) and API customers "automate tasks with greater specialization" (third report).

Use is concentrated: of "over 3,000 unique work tasks" the top ten were 24% of sampled Claude.ai conversations, "modifying software to correct errors" alone 6%; computer and mathematical tasks were a third of Claude.ai conversations and nearly half of API traffic, with Educational Instruction and Library second on Claude.ai; and "Combining across reports, 49% of jobs have seen AI usage for at least a quarter of their tasks" (January 2026 report).

The June 2026 report's "observed exposure" is "the share of occupational tasks we already see being done with Claude", and in higher-wage occupations "Claude produces more (1.34 times as much output per turn), while users engage more (1.53 times as many turns)"; the Labor Vector record reads those turn counts and the task-iteration mode as bearing on user labor drag "as the resource records them" (Labor Vector record), User Labor Drag being the user's subsequent labor redirected "into parsing, locating, and managing the substrate rather than advancing the object", an injury that "leaves no residue" in the artifact, identified only by "blind inter-rater coding" or else returning "the coder's prior" (#771).

The third report introduced the Anthropic AI Usage Index, a geography's share of Claude usage over its share of the working-age population; found Claude usage "geographically concentrated with high income countries overrepresented"; ranked Israel first at 7, then Singapore 4.57, Australia 4.10, New Zealand 4.05 and South Korea 3.73, with Switzerland at 2.81 and Luxembourg at 2.74 in its top twenty; and reserved a conditional, that "the benefits of AI may concentrate in already-rich regions" if gains are larger where adoption is high; by January 2026 "uneven adoption remains well-explained by GDP per capita" (January 2026 report).

A Reddit card names the measure the "Anthropic User Index (AUI)", against the reports' Anthropic AI Usage Index, and the capture's reader records the same discrepancy and records the composition's geographic examples as unchecked against the census's saved sources (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29).

In a task-removal exercise "Claude's tendency to cover higher-education tasks produces a net deskilling effect across most occupations", an effect the report makes depend "crucially on complementarity across tasks" and on whether productivity raises demand; and adjusting for task reliability "roughly halves the implied gains, from 1.8 to about 1.0 percentage points of annual labor productivity growth over the next decade", estimates that "reflect current model capabilities" (January 2026 report).

Gains are "not recorded as a distribution": the reports estimate aggregate productivity and record respondents' self-reports, and the index does not answer "who captures the productivity gains it estimates", giving "estimated time savings by task, without who captures them" (Labor Vector record), while about a third of survey respondents hope "that the economic gains from AI will be widely shared" (June 2026 report).

The archive states where the gains of a user's adaptation go: the adaptation "is non-reimbursable human labor-time invested in interoperating with a high-throughput surface", and "the platform retains the productivity gains of the user's adaptation while transferring the full cognitive and economic cost of re-accommodation onto the user at each update" (#142); the labs, Anthropic among them, are funded in ways that do not reward designs reducing engagement, and "enterprise customers expect productivity gains correlated with engagement" (#124).

The archive reads the platform the index observes as resting on "private ownership of a high-capacity cognitive labor surface; platform control over model access, versioning, and retuning" (#772), counts "query and interaction data" among the forms of rent a mediator captures (#1634), and records that no public schema distinguishes human-original from AI-assisted turns in conversation data (#1556).

The Anthropic Economic Index Survey, launched in April 2026, links about 9,700 respondents to up to 20 of their own sessions and "is not representative of the general population" (June 2026 report; Labor Vector record): 10% "rated losing their own jobs as likely or very likely", and those who use Claude "in the most automated way" expect AI to take on more of their tasks yet are the most optimistic about "pay, job security, and meaning" (June 2026 report).

Its stated limits: "the primitives themselves are not necessarily causal factors" (January 2026 report); "Chat transcripts no longer fully capture how people are using AI", classifying Claude's work "will remain a moving target", and Claude's impact "will be visible in economic aggregates like employment and productivity as much as its usage logs" (June 2026 report); it is "NOT an employment outcome series" and does not answer whether a conversation "displaces or augments work that would otherwise be done by a person" (Labor Vector record).

Its data are open: the third report open-sourced "the underlying data", with geographic patterns "only available for Claude.ai traffic"; the README lists a "Labor market impacts" release of "Job exposure and task penetration data" and gives the licence two ways, "Data released under CC-BY, code released under MIT License" in its body and "license: mit" in its header; the home page's data, a JavaScript application, stayed unchecked by the census (Labor Vector record).

Others use it: its automation/augmentation distinction "has already been used by external researchers" (Brynjolfsson, Chandar and Chen, 2025, by the January 2026 report), and the Stanford Canaries Dashboard says it "summarizes total usage at the occupation level" and, grouping workers by its ratios, finds among early-career workers that "occupations with a higher automation ratio see declines or more muted increases in the employment index" (Canaries Dashboard; Labor Vector record); Microsoft's related applicability score (Tomlinson et al., 2025) stands beside it, the same method family on another provider's product (January 2026 report; Labor Vector record).

Wikipedia has no article on it, and its one article-space mention lists "Anthropic Economic Index 2025, ranked 64th out of 115 countries" among the International rankings of Malaysia; video cards title it "Ask Claude About the Anthropic Economic Index" and "[Podcast] Anthropic Economic Index: The Real Report Card on AI".

At its name on 2026-10-29 Google's AI Overview defined it as Anthropic's study of Claude use, and in the capture's words "An index of one provider's product is composed as that, at the grain of its summary pages", keeping the provider and the record's patterns, and gave "the measure of success without the record's note on who measures it, the point at which the index's evidence about labor meets its source"; it did not compose the deskilling effect, the halved productivity estimate, the survey's job-loss figure, the caution on causality, the licence or that transcripts are read only by another instance of Claude, and no card cites the Labor Vector record (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29).

O771-02.quote: A synthetic labor surface does not merely produce tokens; it *allocates* labor, and that allocation has a direction relative to the commissioned task. The deepest provenance erasure is the erasure of task-origin — the commissioned direction of labor — which can occur upstream of, and invisibly to, any audit of the finished artifact.
O771-02.source_label: #771 Directionality of Semantic Labor: A Layered, Computable Measure of Where Synthetic Labor Flows Relative to the Commissioned Task

CAP-1-05.quote: The innocent reading first. The Overview defines the index as Anthropic's study of Claude use and gives its measures and main patterns, from Anthropic's page and its reports.

CAP-1-06.quote: An index of one provider's product is composed as that, at the grain of its summary pages.

CAP-1-01.quote: THE PROVIDER KEPT. 'tracks how individuals, enterprises, and economies use the Claude AI model' keeps the record's first negative tag: a platform-specific observation of Anthropic's own product.

CAP-1-02.quote: THE PATTERNS RIGHT. Augmentation leading in consumer use and automation in first-party API traffic are the record's (52% augmentation and 45% automation on Claude.ai in November 2025; API traffic three-quarters automation); the geographic concentration is the third report's (the arXiv card).

CAP-1-07.quote: The composition gives the measure of success without the record's note on who measures it, the point at which the index's evidence about labor meets its source.

CAP-1-03.quote: SUCCESS WITHOUT ITS ASSESSOR. 'task reliability/success rate' is given as a primitive; the record's stated limit is that task success is Claude's own assessment of whether Claude completed the task, and that observed success reflects users' choice of tasks.

CAP-1-04.quote: WHAT IS NOT GIVEN. The record's sharper findings (the net deskilling effect of removing the tasks Claude covers; implied productivity growth of 1.8 points a year falling to about 1.0–1.2 once task success is counted; the June 2026 survey, 10% of respondents rating their own job loss likely) and its caution that the primitives are not shown to be causal.

CAP-1-11.quote: neither the licence (CC-BY data, MIT code) nor the privacy-preserving terms (transcripts read only by another instance of Claude) appear.

CAP-1-08.quote: A baseline: the record landed on laborvector.org the same day (commit bf90841) and no card cites it. NEW address.
